reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Strabismus is a misalignment of the visual axes and is described by direction: esotropia (inward), exotropia (outward), hypertropia (upward), and hypotropia (downward)
It is classified as concomitant (the deviation is similar in all directions of gaze, typical of childhood squints) or incomitant (varying with gaze, suggesting a nerve palsy or restriction)
In children the main concern is amblyopia in the deviating eye, whereas new-onset strabismus in adults usually causes diplopia
The cover test (cover-uncover and alternate cover) is the key clinical method for detecting and characterising a manifest or latent deviation
Accommodative esotropia is linked to uncorrected hypermetropia and often improves substantially with the appropriate glasses
A new incomitant squint, especially with a cranial nerve palsy pattern, warrants investigation for a neurological cause
Management principles include correcting refractive error, treating any amblyopia (e.g. occlusion), and surgical realignment of the extraocular muscles when indicated
Leukocoria or a sudden squint in a child requires urgent examination to exclude retinoblastoma or other serious pathology
reference.pathophysiology: Strabismus arises from a failure of the normal binocular alignment maintained by coordinated extraocular muscle action and central fusional control. Causes include refractive error (notably hypermetropia driving accommodative esotropia), sensory deprivation from poor vision in one eye, abnormalities of the neuromuscular pathways (cranial nerve palsies), mechanical restriction of muscles, and disorders of central fusion. In children, misalignment during the critical period of visual development leads to suppression of the deviating eye's image and can result in amblyopia and loss of binocular single vision.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudostrabismus from prominent epicanthic folds or facial asymmetry
Cranial nerve palsy (third, fourth, or sixth nerve)
Restrictive myopathy (e.g. thyroid eye disease, orbital fracture)
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia and other supranuclear disorders
Retinoblastoma or other cause of sensory deprivation in a child
additionalInvestigations: Cover-uncover and alternate cover tests to detect and measure the deviation
Assessment of visual acuity in each eye to detect amblyopia
Cycloplegic refraction to identify a correctable refractive cause
Ocular motility examination and assessment of binocular function/stereopsis
Neuroimaging when an incomitant or paralytic squint suggests a neurological lesion
redFlags: New-onset incomitant squint with features of a cranial nerve palsy suggesting intracranial pathology
Leukocoria or a squint accompanying poor vision in a child, raising concern for retinoblastoma
Sudden diplopia with headache or other neurological signs
Painful or restricted eye movements suggesting orbital or inflammatory disease
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are generally favourable when strabismus and any associated amblyopia are detected and treated early in childhood, with good prospects for alignment and, in some cases, binocular vision; late detection reduces the chance of restoring binocularity, and adult acquired strabismus depends on the underlying cause.
pitfalls: Dismissing a genuine squint as pseudostrabismus and delaying amblyopia treatment
Failing to perform cycloplegic refraction and missing correctable accommodative esotropia
Not investigating a new incomitant or paralytic squint for a neurological cause
Overlooking a serious underlying cause such as retinoblastoma in a child presenting with a squint
management: Correct refractive error, particularly hypermetropia, with spectacles for accommodative esotropia
Treat amblyopia in children with occlusion (patching) or atropine penalisation of the better-seeing eye
Prisms incorporated into spectacles to relieve diplopia in acquired adult strabismus
Extraocular muscle surgery to realign the visual axes where non-surgical measures are insufficient
Botulinum toxin injection to extraocular muscles in selected cases
Investigate and manage any underlying neurological cause of an incomitant or paralytic squint
Orthoptic assessment and long-term follow-up of alignment, binocular function and stereopsis
